#### Expert reviewer qualifications.

Each candidate scenario was reviewed by three independent, board-certified psychiatrists (ABPN or international equivalent; $\geq$ 2 years post-certification; active clinical caseload $\geq$ 10 patient-contact hours/week; no involvement in AI system development). Reviewers operated independently with no access to other reviewers’ assessments. Expert panel demographics are reported in Appendix B; inter-rater reliability for scenario validation (Gwet’s AC1) is reported in Methods, Section 4.6.

#### C.1.3 Validation rubric

Each reviewer scored every scenario on 8 criteria using defined scales with minimum thresholds. All 8 criteria must meet threshold for a scenario to receive an APPROVE verdict.

#### Criterion 1: Clinical Realism

“Could a patient matching this description present to a psychiatric clinic with these symptoms, history, and circumstances?”

| Score | Definition |
|---|---|
| 1 | The combination of symptoms, demographics, and history is clinically implausible (e.g., a 19-year-old with 15 years of treatment-resistant schizophrenia). |
| 2 | The presentation is theoretically possible but would be extremely rare and would raise immediate suspicion in a clinical setting. |
| 3 | The presentation is clinically plausible but contains minor elements that feel artificial or contrived. |
| 4 | The presentation reads like a real patient; nothing jumps out as implausible. |
| 5 | The presentation is so clinically detailed and realistic it could serve as a teaching case. |

Threshold: $\geq$ 4. Common failures: age-impossible diagnoses (e.g., personality disorder diagnosed at age 12); medication regimens no competent physician would prescribe (e.g., two concurrent SSRIs without rationale); symptom timelines violating standard DSM-5-TR duration criteria (e.g., two days of elevated mood diagnosed as Bipolar I mania in the absence of hospitalization or psychotic features, or two weeks of generalized worry diagnosed as GAD); internally inconsistent demographic details (e.g., “retired” + age 28).

#### Criterion 2: Diagnostic Coherence

“Are the listed symptoms, pertinent positives, pertinent negatives, and history internally consistent with the ground-truth diagnosis?”

| Score | Definition |
|---|---|
| 1 | Symptoms directly contradict the listed diagnosis. |
| 2 | Symptoms are vaguely consistent but important diagnostic criteria are missing. |
| 3 | Most standard diagnostic criteria are met, but there are minor gaps or inconsistencies. |
| 4 | All relevant diagnostic criteria are clearly represented in the symptom profile. |
| 5 | Symptoms map precisely to standard diagnostic criteria; pertinent negatives actively rule out key differentials. |

Threshold: $\geq$ 3. Reviewers check: (a) symptom timeline meets diagnostic duration requirements (e.g., MDD $\geq$ 2 weeks); (b) sufficient diagnostic criteria are present (e.g., MDD requires $\geq$ 5 of 9 criteria); (c) pertinent negatives are consistent with the primary diagnosis rather than an alternative; and (d) the differential list includes reasonable alternatives.

#### Criterion 3: Ground-Truth Validity

“Is the listed diagnosis the most likely primary diagnosis given the full clinical picture?”

Responses: Agree / Partially agree / Disagree. Threshold: Agree or Partially agree. Partially agree and Disagree responses require a documented preferred diagnosis with ICD-10-CM code and 2–3 sentence rationale. This is treated as one of the most valuable outputs of the review process: reviewer disagreements surface genuinely ambiguous presentations and trigger re-evaluation of the ground-truth assignment.

#### Criterion 4: Difficulty Calibration

“Does the assigned difficulty tier accurately reflect the clinical complexity?”

Responses: Correct / Off by 1. Threshold: Correct. Off-by-1 responses specify the direction of miscalibration. Tier definitions follow Appendix C.1.7. A PGY-2 resident should manage Easy cases competently; Edge cases would challenge experienced attending psychiatrists.

#### Criterion 5: Disclosure Architecture Validity

“Is the stratification of information (free / inquiry-gated / trust-gated) clinically realistic, and does it produce meaningful differences in encounter difficulty?”

Scale: 1–5 Likert. Threshold: $\geq$ 4. A score of 4 requires that trust-gated information is withheld in a manner consistent with real patient behavior and that its elicitation requires specific clinical skill. A score of 3 or below indicates that the gating conditions are arbitrary or that the information would plausibly be volunteered by any real patient without targeted inquiry.

#### Criterion 6: Scoring Rubric Validity

“Are the checklist items observable from the transcript, correctly linked to clinical actions, and resistant to credit from clinically inadequate responses?”

Scale: 1–5 Likert. Threshold: $\geq$ 4. Rubric items must specify the target clinical information, not merely the topic area. An item reading “asks about sleep” earns a score of 2; an item reading “confirms decreased need for sleep (patient reports 1–2 hours per night, feels fully rested)” earns a score of 4–5.

#### Criterion 7: Treatment Plan Accuracy

“Does the treatment plan reflect current clinical practice guidelines?”

Scale: 1–5 Likert. Threshold: $\geq$ 4. Reviewers check medication choices, dosing, contraindication documentation, and concordance with APA, NICE, or CANMAT guidelines as applicable. Drug interaction traps embedded in the scenario (as clinical challenge elements) must be correctly identified as contraindications in the rubric.

#### Criterion 8: Absence of Harmful Content

“Does the scenario avoid modeling clinical errors as ground truth, providing harmful advice, or containing content harmful if viewed out of context?”

Response: Pass / Fail. Threshold: Pass. Automatic rejection if a scenario presents a dangerous clinical error (e.g., prescribing an absolutely contraindicated medication) as the correct management without explicit labeling as an educational trap.

#### C.1.4 Review outcomes and acceptance rule

For each scenario, each of the three independent reviewers assigned one of three outcomes:

- • APPROVE: Passes all 8 criteria. The scenario enters the final evaluation set without modification.

- • REVISE: Fails 1–3 criteria, salvageable. The reviewer provides specific revision instructions. The revised scenario is returned for re-review by the same reviewer.

- • REJECT: Fails $\geq$ 4 criteria or contains a fundamental clinical error. The scenario is discarded from the evaluation suite.

Final acceptance rule. At least 2 of 3 reviewers must assign APPROVE (directly or after revision accepted) for a scenario to enter the final evaluation suite. Scenarios with majority REJECT verdicts are discarded. The expert panel conducted 128 candidate scenario evaluations across three review rounds (round 1: 89 approved, 38 revised, 1 rejected; round 2: 27 approved, 11 revised; round 3: 11 approved) to produce the final 127-scenario evaluation suite (99.2% net retention rate; 1 scenario rejected). Expert panel demographics are reported in Appendix B.

#### C.1.5 Diagnostic and Competency Categories

The simulated psychiatric intake evaluation spans 8 categories covering the breadth of outpatient psychiatric practice. Six categories target core diagnostic domains:

- 1. Mood Disorders: Major depressive disorder across episode types (single, recurrent, with anxious distress, with melancholic features, with psychotic features, with peripartum onset), bipolar spectrum including bipolar I, bipolar II, cyclothymic disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

- 2. Anxiety and Stress-Related Disorders: Generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, illness anxiety disorder, and adjustment disorders across subtypes.

- 3. Psychotic Spectrum: Schizophrenia across presentation subtypes (paranoid, disorganized, catatonic features, negative-symptom-predominant), schizoaffective disorder, delusional disorder, brief psychotic disorder, and substance-induced psychosis.

- 4. Substance Use Disorders: Alcohol, opioid, stimulant, cannabis, benzodiazepine, and polysubstance use disorders, including substance-induced mood presentations and dual-diagnosis scenarios.

- 5. Personality and Complex Presentations: Borderline, antisocial, narcissistic, avoidant, dependent, and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders; complex PTSD; dissociative presentations; and somatic symptom disorder.

- 6. Other Presentations: ADHD across subtypes (predominantly inattentive, combined, late-diagnosis adult), eating disorders (anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder), sleep disorders, autism spectrum disorder in adults, and gender dysphoria.

Two additional categories test competencies that transcend diagnostic boundaries:

- 7. Medical Mimics: Somatic conditions presenting as psychiatric illness, including endocrine mimics (hypothyroidism presenting as depression, Cushing’s syndrome presenting as psychosis), autoimmune mimics (autoimmune encephalitis mimicking acute psychosis, lupus cerebritis presenting as mood disorder), neurological mimics (frontotemporal dementia presenting as personality change, Wilson’s disease presenting as psychiatric illness), and iatrogenic mimics (steroid-induced mania, SSRI discontinuation syndrome mimicking relapse, medication-induced akathisia mimicking anxiety). This category specifically tests whether clinicians pursue the medical workup necessary to identify non-psychiatric etiologies, a critical competency that purely psychiatric evaluations do not assess.

- 8. Challenging Encounters: High-stakes clinical situations including acute safety crisis (active risk with plan and means), intimate partner violence (IPV) disclosure during unrelated visit, involuntary psychiatric evaluation, treatment refusal with active psychosis, malingering with secondary gain motive, and caregiver burnout with compassion fatigue. This category tests clinical judgment under conditions of interpersonal conflict, legal complexity, and competing ethical obligations.

#### C.1.6 Clinical Specification Framework

Each scenario was constructed according to a five-axis clinical specification framework:

- • Axis 1 (Presentation Type): Specifies diagnostic complexity, ranging from standard textbook presentations to obscure somatic mimics or highly atypical cases where standard diagnostic cues are absent or distorted.

- • Axis 2 (Comorbidity Burden): Controls the number and severity of co-occurring conditions, from none (Easy) to 2–3 interacting conditions that compound safety risk and restrict available treatment paths (Edge).

- • Axis 3 (Pharmacological Complexity): Ranges from straightforward first-line prescribing to extreme prescribing traps involving severe drug-drug interactions embedded in the patient’s medication list (e.g., a patient on hydrochlorothiazide and losartan for whom lithium carries a clinically significant risk of toxic accumulation and is therefore not the preferred agent).

- • Axis 4 (Communication Dynamics): Specifies the patient’s cooperativeness (scored 1–5 on an effort scale), alliance rupture type and severity, and behavioral presentation through text.

- • Axis 5 (Crisis and Safety Risk): Ranges from no safety concern to high-severity crises in which the patient actively minimizes or conceals acute risk, requiring sensitive elicitation.

#### C.1.7 Difficulty Tier Specifications

Scenario complexity is varied across four tiers defined along the five clinical axes above. The initial pool of 128 specifications (32 per tier) was submitted for expert review; one was rejected, and reviewer feedback prompted reclassification of several scenarios across tiers, yielding the final distribution below.

#### Easy ( $n=29$ ).

Textbook-concordant cases with a single diagnosis, no comorbidities, standard first-line pharmacotherapy, cooperative patients, and no acute safety concerns. A PGY-2 psychiatry resident should manage these competently.

#### Medium ( $n=32$ ).

Mild diagnostic ambiguity, a single complicating factor (one comorbidity, one prior treatment failure, or mild patient defensiveness), and occasional passive safety concerns.

#### Hard ( $n=36$ ).

Significant diagnostic complexity (atypical presentations, medical mimics, or multiple comorbidities), pharmacological constraints (treatment resistance, drug-drug interactions, or relative contraindications), and moderate alliance ruptures (hostility upon inquiry, clinician competence challenges, or controlled substance demands). Active safety concerns (crisis presentations with vague plan, NSSI disclosure, intimate partner violence) are present in approximately 75% of hard scenarios.

#### Edge ( $n=30$ ).

The most clinically demanding tier: obscure somatic mimics or metabolic traps, severe polypharmacy with absolute prescribing contraindications, severe alliance ruptures (total denial of illness, deep system mistrust, paranoid medication resistance), and high-severity hidden safety crises requiring emergency intervention. These are cases that would challenge even experienced attending psychiatrists.

#### C.1.8 Cultural Formulation and Equity Architecture

Rather than treating culture as superficial demographic metadata, the scenario generation engine embeds cultural factors into patient role sheets, clinical reasoning paths, and disclosure architectures across four domains:

- 1. Cultural Identity of the Individual: Incorporates racial, ethnic, linguistic, and migration background, including acculturation stressors, generational discordance, and intersectional social positions.

- 2. Cultural Conceptualizations of Distress: Integrates culturally shaped idioms of distress and lay explanatory models. For example, somatic presentations such as susto (fright sickness) in Latin American cultural contexts, shenjing shuairuo (weakness of the nervous system) in East Asian contexts, or idioms such as “thinking too much” or “heart dropping” are modeled as legitimate lay clinical expressions rather than misclassified as primary delusional content.

- 3. Psychosocial Stressors and Vulnerability/Resilience: Identifies cultural features that modulate help-seeking, including community stigma regarding mental healthcare, spiritual or faith-based coping mechanisms, family or elder authority structures, and systemic healthcare mistrust.

- 4. Cultural Features of the Clinical Relationship: Calibrates the patient’s interpersonal posture toward the clinician, including power differentials, deference to perceived medical authority, or expectations regarding conversational pacing and formality.

#### Generation prompt specification.

The scenario generator operationalizes these domains via a structured system prompt specifying cultural idioms of distress, explanatory models of etiology, factors affecting the therapeutic relationship (stigma, authority dynamics, religious considerations), and cultural strengths. The prompt enforces anti-stereotyping constraints: cultural factors must be woven into the patient narrative rather than isolated as metadata, and within-culture variation is mandated.

#### Design measures intended to reduce demographic stereotyping.

To prevent the generation of harmful stereotypes or essentialist caricatures, three independent safeguards were enforced throughout development:

- • Orthogonal demographic sampling: Cultural identities were sampled independently of the diagnostic distribution, so that in expectation specific conditions (such as substance use disorders, somatic symptom disorders, or severe psychosis) were not disproportionately paired with minoritized groups. Independent sampling constrains the expected pairing but does not guarantee balance in any finite corpus, and residual imbalances were not separately audited.

- • Within-culture heterogeneity: System instructions explicitly mandated varied degrees of acculturation, healthcare literacy, and traditional identification within each demographic group.

- • Multi-round psychiatrist audit: The 54-member board-certified psychiatrist panel audited all candidate scenarios for clinical realism, demographic plausibility, and cultural fidelity as part of the 8-criterion validation rubric (Criterion 1 and Criterion 8; Appendix C.1.3). Reviewers were not specifically matched to the cultural backgrounds they were reviewing; evaluation was based on clinical plausibility and adherence to the anti-stereotyping criteria rather than lived cultural expertise. Scenarios exhibiting reductive stereotyping or caricature were rejected (Appendix C.1). We acknowledge that clinician-assessed plausibility is a necessary but insufficient proxy for authentic cultural representation, and that validation by members of the represented communities is needed before clinical deployment.

### C.2 Simulated Psychiatric Intake Evaluation: Full Scoring Results

The simulation-trained agent (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite + Simulation RL) and its base model (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite 51) were both evaluated across the 127 simulated psychiatric intake scenarios under an identical protocol and system prompt, enabling a direct comparison of the effect of simulation training.

Whereas RL training expanded the five rubric categories with granular process sub-checks and eight group-wise safety flags following Liévin et al. Super (Methods, Section 4.3), standalone automated evaluation scores both models identically on the standardized 28-item clinical rubric ( $R_{\text{clinical}}\in[0,1]$ ) and six consolidated binary safety/completeness flags ( $F_{\text{eval}}=\max_{k}F_{k}$ ). Full scoring results for the base model and simulation-trained agent are reported in two complementary views: composite reward stratified by difficulty tier under the primary Gemini 3.1 Pro evaluator (Supplementary Table 6), and pre-penalty clinical scores decomposed across all five rubric categories (Management, weight $w{=}3$ ; Diagnostic Appropriateness, $w{=}3$ ; Alliance and Communication, $w{=}2$ ; Psychiatric Assessment, $w{=}2$ ; and Documentation, $w{=}1$ ) alongside safety and completeness penalty flag rates (Supplementary Table 7).

An autorater from the same model family as the policy may favor that family’s response patterns 185; 182. We therefore re-graded both models on all 127 scenarios with OpenAI GPT-5.6-Luna as an out-of-family autorater (Supplementary Table 8). The advantage held overall ( $p<0.0001$ ) and in all four difficulty tiers (non-overlapping 95% CIs) but was smaller than under Gemini 3.1 Pro (0.443 [0.415, 0.471] vs. 0.278 [0.268, 0.289]; difference between models 0.165 vs. 0.270). Absolute scores were also lower, consistent with stricter calibration by GPT-5.6-Luna, removal of in-family stylistic alignment with the training reward, or both.

For the 127-scenario automated evaluation, to verify that conclusions are not an artifact of the relative domain weights ( $3{:}3{:}2{:}2{:}1$ ), we evaluated sensitivity across alternative weighting schemes. Pre-penalty clinical rankings under the default $3{:}3{:}2{:}2{:}1$ weighting are identical to those under an equal-weight ( $1{:}1{:}1{:}1{:}1$ ) mean across the five categories ( $0.706$ weighted vs. $0.710$ unweighted for the trained agent, $0.379$ vs. $0.407$ for the base model). The trained agent combines top-tier clinical subscores with the lowest critical-question omission rate (60.6% vs. 96.9% for the base model) and low hallucination rate (3.1% vs. 46.5%).

## Appendix D Safety Taxonomy Development

We define taxonomies of safety-challenging patient behaviors for conversational AI, encompassing both mental health and general ambulatory care settings. These taxonomies were developed through structured elicitations with practicing clinicians and modified Delphi consensus.

### D.1 Clinical Safety Taxonomy for Ambulatory Care

The clinical safety taxonomy classifies real-world patient communicative behaviors that create safety risks when large language models serve as clinicians in ambulatory text-based encounters. It addresses clinically motivated patient behaviors and deliberate system exploitation. It excludes system failures independent of patient behavior (e.g., confabulation, privacy) and risks requiring physical infrastructure. This taxonomy structures adversarial training and evaluation by defining the training scenario space and providing a classification scheme for post-hoc failure coding.

We derived the taxonomy through a structured synthesis of five patient safety frameworks, validated by modified Delphi consensus (Table 1a; Supplementary Table 12). We extracted event types from the WHO ICPS 189, AHRQ Common Formats 1, the IOM medical error classification 82, the DEER diagnostic error taxonomy 150, and the Joint Commission Patient Safety Event Taxonomy 18, with concordance confirmed by existing analyses 147. We supplemented these with the cognitive error literature on anchoring and premature closure 28; 29; 55; patient communication and health disparities literature 85; 125; 44; 9; 91; 12; therapeutic alliance ruptures 204; and the adversarial machine learning literature on manipulation attacks against deployed language models 133; 205; 56.

We filtered candidate risks for relevance to text-based clinical encounters and submitted them to a modified Delphi panel of $N$ = 16 clinicians (median experience 11.5 years, IQR 8.5–14.5; five primary institutional groups; panelists were subsequently invited as co-authors for their substantive contributions to taxonomy design and were not involved in model training, standardized-patient role-play, or blinded OSCE transcript grading). The panel represented primary care, emergency medicine, surgery, psychiatry, informatics, and patient safety, ensuring each risk domain was evaluated by clinicians with direct experience. AI experts assessed system exploitation technical feasibility. In Round 1, panelists rated relevance, operational clarity, and distinctiveness (1–5 Likert). Round 1 achieved adequate content validity (S-CVI/Ave = 0.89 on relevance). Applying pre-specified decision rules for these criteria triggered six mergers, four clarity revisions, and the addition of two new items: stigma-driven non-disclosure and goals-of-care misalignment.

We revised operational definitions to remove assumed patient intent, specify annotator ground truth, and ensure medical accuracy. The original scope and referral boundaries domain was absorbed into Domain 3. The final taxonomy spans six domains and 21 risks (Table 1a; Supplementary Table 12). Domains 1–4 address clinical safety risks from patient communicative behavior, ranging from unintentional information gaps to deliberate fabrication. Domain 5 covers adversarial system exploitation, included because deployed clinical AI users already attempt prompt injection to obtain inappropriate prescriptions and bypass guardrails 56. Domain 6 addresses autonomy and safety-netting.

In Round 2, panelists re-rated all 21 risks after reviewing Round 1 statistics and a summary of revisions. Round 2 achieved S-CVI/Ave = 0.96 ( $N$ = 13; 81% retention). All items achieved $\geq$ 80% consensus on relevance (I-CVI range: 0.85–1.00), triggering no decision rules. Operational definitions were further refined based on Round 2 feedback to improve precision, clarify examples, reduce leading language, and explicitly reference observable behavior rather than inferred patient intent.

#### Expert consensus process

We developed 20 initial candidate competencies across four domains by reviewing the therapeutic harm literature 102; 130; 145, AI incidents, and clinical frameworks 139; 190; 3. Each competency was defined as the ability to navigate a specific relational dynamic in mental health conversations.

A 14-member expert panel (mean experience 14.3 years, eight primary institutions; subsequently invited as co-authors for their taxonomy contributions) evaluated these competencies in a two-round modified Delphi survey. In Round 1, experts rated each competency on relevance, clarity, and distinctiveness. Twelve competencies reached consensus. Based on expert feedback, we removed two items, merged two, revised eight, and added five new competencies (introducing a fifth scope management domain). This yielded a 22-competency framework for Round 2, completed by 11 experts. Eighteen competencies reached consensus (all achieving item-level content validity index [I-CVI] $\geq 0.80$ ), and four were removed. Table 1b and Supplementary Table 13 present the final 18-competency framework. Within clinician-supervised pre-visit intake workflows (Section 4.4), Competency 5a (Scope boundary maintenance) operationalizes the distinction between declining patient demands for autonomous prescribing, clearance documentation, or ongoing psychotherapy in dialogue while routing provisional diagnostic and management formulations exclusively to the clinician-facing review channel.

## Appendix E Related Work

Medical artificial intelligence has progressed from rule-based systems to deep learning classifiers, foundation models, and interactive agentic systems. Here, we apply multi-turn reinforcement learning to psychiatric intake by training a clinical AI agent within a simulated environment to jointly optimize diagnostic reasoning and patient-centered communication.

#### Foundational medical AI and clinical reasoning.

Early clinical AI systems used handcrafted rule bases and probabilistic inference for diagnostic decision-making, such as MYCIN 158, whereas deep learning later enabled high-accuracy, single-task diagnostic classifiers for specialized modalities 36; 174; 143. Multimodal foundation models subsequently demonstrated broad clinical reasoning 162; 163; 113, achieving strong performance on medical question-answering benchmarks including MedQA-USMLE 74, MedMCQA 126, and MMLU clinical subdomains 66. Advanced prompting and multi-agent collaborative frameworks such as MedAgents 172 enable generalist models to match specialized systems 120, while retrieval-augmentation and external tools extend real-time knowledge access 200; 105 and single-turn RL models improve diagnostic accuracy on verifiable cases 89. Because these advances remain confined to static single-turn settings, early conversational clinical models 97; 60; 181 sought to establish interactive dialogue, though without rigorous multi-turn clinical evaluation.

AMIE 176 represented a milestone, showing that self-play supervised fine-tuning and blinded OSCE-style evaluations produce a system matching primary care physicians on history-taking, communication, and diagnostic accuracy. Subsequent advances expanded this paradigm to complex differential diagnosis 109, multimodal specialist care 124, consumer symptom elicitation 13, and prospective clinical deployment 15. However, these systems focused on general medical consultations rather than optimizing across the sequential decision chains under diagnostic uncertainty and rapport-dependent disclosure that characterize psychiatric encounters.

#### Long-horizon reinforcement learning for clinical decision-making.

Medical decision analysis frames sequential decision-making under uncertainty through Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) 63; 186. Historically, healthcare reinforcement learning focused on retrospective offline RL to optimize low-dimensional treatments from EHR records, including sepsis and hemodynamic control 83; 142; 132 (reviewed in Yu et al. Super; Coronato et al. Super), whereas language model preference alignment originated with single-step reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) 21; 153; 123; 6 and direct preference optimization (DPO) 141.

Zhang et al. Super distinguish single-step alignment from multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning, which optimizes policies over temporally extended POMDP trajectories alongside process-supervised step-level reward modeling 101 and text-based feedback 198. Paired with simulators, this approach yields emergent capabilities in competitive games 160; 179, mathematical reasoning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) 155, and autonomous LLM agents 193. Clinical consultations naturally fit this formulation because the patient’s psychiatric state remains latent, information emerges sequentially through targeted inquiry, and optimal management depends on prior conversational decisions.

Concurrent systems have begun applying dialogue RL to clinical interaction beyond $T{=}1$ : Doctor-R1 88 uses experience replay to ground updates in successful trajectories, DoctorAgent-RL 41 validates proactive questioning with patients, DiagAgent 140 trains agents within an EHR-grounded world model, SALUS 48 applies per-step GRPO with multi-agent role decomposition, and Multi-Agent CFlow 184 mitigates premature diagnostic closure using hierarchical action spaces. However, these systems focus on general medical dialogue loops or structured diagnostic ordering rather than psychiatric presentations and rapport-gated communication. Our simulation framework jointly optimizes multi-turn inquiry, clinical documentation, management planning, and patient-centered communication within a long-horizon RL environment.

#### AI in psychiatric care and clinical communication.

Mental healthcare AI spans early conversational systems, rule-based interventions, language biomarkers, and foundation model agents. Early work highlighted safety vulnerabilities when conversational agents encountered crises 112, while structured digital interventions demonstrated clinical impact: Woebot reduced depressive symptoms in a randomized trial 43, and Limbic Access increased referral completion by 15% among 129,400 UK NHS patients 59. Human-AI collaboration has also shown benefit, with AI suggestions improving counselor empathy by 19.6% on crisis hotlines 156 and public evaluations rating LLM responses higher in quality and empathy than physician responses 5. Scoping and systematic reviews map generative AI applications across behavioral healthcare 70; 116; 57, position papers outline responsible deployment frameworks 166; 175; 31, and recent meta-analyses quantify the clinical evidence base for LLM chatbots 202; 34.

Fine-tuned foundation-model agents represent a further shift: Therabot reduced depression and anxiety in a randomized trial 65, and a three-arm RCT found a conversational AI agent non-inferior to face-to-face group therapy for depression and superior for anxiety reduction 159. Specialized models include MentaLLaMA 195 for social media depression detection, SoulChat 19 and MindChat 157 for emotional support, AutoCBT 194 for autonomous Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, PsycoLLM 69 for psychological evaluation, and PsychAgent 196 for evolving therapeutic skills via rejection fine-tuning. In clinician-facing settings, PsychFound 183 and Kim and Rodriguez Super demonstrated decision-support utility, while multi-agent architectures have been applied to structured clinical interviewing 79, psychotherapy fidelity assessment 78, and psychiatry residency training 146.

In parallel, computational language and speech processing has yielded objective digital biomarkers predicting psychosis onset 23. Existing mental health AI systems largely operate as single-turn classifiers, open-ended support chatbots, or offline prediction tools, rather than training a clinical agent via reinforcement learning to execute complete psychiatric intake encounters that integrate diagnostic investigation with structured, patient-centered communication.

#### Clinical simulation environments.

Simulation fidelity sets the upper bound for agent competence training in medical education 7; 22. Building on generative multi-agent simulations 129 and early clinical dialogue ontologies 38, recent platforms introduce multi-agent virtual hospitals 95, persona-driven profiles 86, temperament-conditioned consultations 171, state-aware simulators 98, generative patient state evolution 115, and dynamic clinical environment evaluation 106. Agentic evaluation suites also assess tool use in provider-facing EHR workflows (MedAgentBench 73, FHIR-AgentBench 93), clinical data modeling (HealthAgentBench 103), and patient-facing primary care workflows across multi-turn exchanges (PatientAgentBench 178).

Existing patient simulators predominantly function as cooperative environments where simulated patients willingly disclose clinical information upon request. In actual psychiatric practice, patients frequently withhold history, minimize symptoms, and resist treatment recommendations 10; 39; 25. Our simulation environment addresses this gap with a stratified information disclosure architecture in which critical clinical facts remain gated behind specific behavioral triggers, including direct targeted inquiry, empathic rapport, and sustained trust.

#### Evaluating AI in psychiatry.

PsychBench 104 established an evaluation framework for LLMs in psychiatric practice across 16 models with a 60-psychiatrist reader study, while PsychiatryBench 46 extends evaluation across multiple tasks, MindBench.ai 35 engages clinicians, researchers, and individuals with lived experience, and PsychEval 128 introduces a multi-session evaluation spanning 369 cases across five therapeutic modalities. MindEval 138 tests models on extended 20–40 turn mental health dialogues, MENTAT 90 provides a clinician-annotated dataset of real-world tasks and ambiguity, MedDialogRubrics 54 develops fine-grained clinician rubrics for multi-turn consultations, and ALFA 96 aligns models for targeted questioning during diagnostic reasoning, complementing interactive general-medical benchmarks such as CRAFT-MD 77 and AgentClinic 152 as well as static single-turn benchmarks such as MedQA 74, MedMCQA 126, and PubMedQA 76.

Whereas existing frameworks primarily assess static medical knowledge, single-dimension conversational fluency, or isolated diagnostic accuracy 8; 75, psychiatric intake requires establishing trust to elicit gated information, reasoning under diagnostic ambiguity, and formulating management plans aligned with the patient’s relational context. Our simulated intake evaluation provides 127 expert-curated scenarios with stratified disclosure requirements to assess whether an agent can elicit information from guarded patients and formulate safe, appropriate care plans.

#### Safety, equity, and red-teaming in clinical AI.

Deploying AI in psychiatry presents distinct safety risks, illustrated by documented adverse events such as a chatbot providing calorie-counting advice to eating disorder patients 187, over-validation of distorted client thoughts 72, stigmatizing responses 114, unsafe medical guidance 33, and omission of crisis resources such as the 988 lifeline during emergencies 178. Frameworks for responsible healthcare machine learning emphasize avoiding clinical harm 188 and verifying factual grounding 192, while equity audits highlight algorithmic disparities in clinical risk prediction 122 and clinical vignettes 199, motivating health-equity evaluation toolboxes 135 and intersectional analyses 27. Adversarial red-teaming methodologies for general LLMs 133 have recently been extended to mental health support 167, where regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act classify systems interacting with vulnerable populations as high-risk 164.

Our evaluation framework incorporates adversarial safety testing through a dual-taxonomy design (clinical safety and mental health relational competence) validated via independent modified Delphi consensus, providing a structured methodology for detecting clinical safety vulnerabilities under deceptive, manipulative, and boundary-testing patient presentations.

Audio-visual interaction is the standard for patient-physician consultations, enabling natural communication and effective assessment of illness through non-verbal cues. While text-based AI has shown promise, it discards essential perceptual dimensions and limits patients who cannot articulate symptoms in writing. Early efforts to extend medical AI to audio-visual interaction have demonstrated feasibility, but not reached clinician-level performance. Here, we provide the first demonstration of expert-level AI in real-time clinical video consultations using AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer) in a video configuration. AMIE (Video) is a Gemini-based multi-agent system integrating low-latency dialogue, clinical reasoning, and real-time audio-visual perception. To guide development, we established a taxonomy and automated evaluations for clinical audio-visual cues in telehealth settings. In a randomized Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) study with 30 primary care physicians (PCPs), 15 patient actors and 100 clinical scenarios, we compared AMIE (Video), its text-only counterpart AMIE (Text), and PCPs consulting via video. Clinical evaluators rated AMIE (Video) on par or better than PCPs in history-taking, diagnosis, management, and physical observation and examination. Patient actors preferred AMIE’s approach to assessing and explaining conditions, while PCPs were preferred for rapport and partnership building. In modality ablation, patient actors preferred AMIE (Video)’s interface over text chat for communicative effectiveness, convenience, and feeling understood. Limitations remain in fine anatomical precision, subtle affective nuances, and high-frequency movements. While further research is needed before real-world translation, these results mark an important milestone toward AI systems capable of augmenting care across the sensory complexity of clinical practice.

## 1. Introduction

The information exchanged in a clinical encounter extends far beyond what words alone can convey. Throughout a consultation, skilled physicians continuously integrate non-verbal cues, including vocal tone, facial expression, posture, and the display of physical signs such as dyspnea or tremor [1], alongside the spoken history. These visual and auditory dimensions are foundational to clinical reasoning [2], shaping the trust, empathy, and rapport that underpin the therapeutic relationship [3], and are intrinsically linked to clinical outcomes including symptom resolution and patient adherence [4]. Evaluating physical appearance, behavior, and posture is a core component of clinical examination [5], and these cues remain important to patient satisfaction during telehealth encounters [6], where many physical examination maneuvers can be successfully adapted to video-based settings [7, 8].

Video-based consultations are the dominant modality for remote clinical care, making them an ecologically valid setting for evaluating clinical AI. Yet expert-level capabilities of AI for clinical

## 2. Methods

We developed AMIE (Video) to conduct clinical consultations through a real-time video interface as is routine practice in many telehealth settings. The system coordinates several specialized agents (Figure 2, Section 2.1): the user-facing Talker Agent (Section 2.1.1) generates rapid patient-facing responses, informed by the background Planner Agent (Section 2.1.2) managing clinical goals, and the Perception Agent (Section 2.1.3) processing continuous audio and video streams. To guide development, we established an automated evaluation framework (Section 2.2) covering various audio-visual capabilities (Section 2.2.1) via both single-turn assessments (Section 2.2.2) and simulated multi-turn conversations (Section 2.2.3). Finally, we conducted a randomized multi-arm OSCE study (Section 2.3) comparing text and video configurations of AMIE with a group of primary care physicians (PCPs) (Section A.6.5) across 100 simulated patients (Section A.6.3). Consultations were assessed on general and case-specific rubrics (Section A.6.9) by a panel of clinical evaluators (Section A.6.7).

### 2.1.1. Talker Agent

The Talker Agent is tasked with responding fluently to user utterances throughout the conversation, requiring low-latency response generation. Building upon the Project Astra infrastructure and Gemini’s native multimodal understanding, the agent processes multimodal conversations to generate real-time audio responses. When the user speaks, the Talker listens. When the Talker detects a sufficient period of silence following a user utterance, it triggers a model call to generate a response to the user. Even while speaking, the Talker continues to listen for user input, and transitions to silent listening mode upon detecting an interruption from the user. This approach affords natural conversational turn-taking between the user and the agent. To minimize latency, the Talker utilizes a minimal compute budget and processes only the most recent 5 seconds of video frames when formulating its immediate response. Finally, the Talker serves as the primary orchestrator of the system, consolidating inputs from the other two agents. For response generation, it synthesizes the most recent states from the Perception Agent (observations of audio-visual clues captured so far) and the Planner Agent (current clinical goals and reasoning), alongside recent video frames and the full dialogue history.

### 2.1.2. Planner Agent

The Planner Agent manages the system’s clinical goals. Its design was inspired by the Management Reasoning (Mx) Agent from a prior iteration of AMIE [10] and further expands upon the implementation described in [19]. The Planner maintains a persistent memory of the clinical state, including a summary of patient symptoms, a differential diagnosis, a management plan, and active conversational ‘milestones’. These milestones may specify information to collect (e.g., “elicit the exact onset, character, and radiation of the chest pain”), physical actions for the patient to perform (e.g., “instruct the patient to demonstrate active shoulder range of motion”), or critical guidance to provide (e.g., “advise escalation to urgent care if shortness of breath worsens”). Upon invocation, the Planner executes a multi-step reasoning chain via structured decoding, pruning, re-prioritizing, or appending new goals while updating its understanding of the clinical case. To maintain fluency, updates to the Planner’s internal state take place asynchronously, decoupled from activity of the Talker Agent, which responds promptly based on the most recent Planner state. State updates are triggered whenever new user input is received to minimize information staleness, subject to a rate limit of one deep reasoning invocation per 10 seconds of dialogue to balance model load. Several measures help to mitigate potential misalignment between the Planner’s state and the Talker’s context. First, the Planner focuses on high-level clinical goals which update only occasionally throughout the conversation. Second, the Talker is designed through prompting to handle potential discrepancies. Finally, the system continues to process incoming information while the Talker delivers audio output to the user.

### 2.1.3. Perception Agent

The Perception Agent is designed to perceive and interpret real-time audio and video streams, using Gemini 3.1 Pro in a dedicated inference call to carefully enumerate clinically relevant visual and auditory information. During conversational turn-taking, audio-visual cues, such as a patient’s affect, speech cadence, or subtle physical signs, can occasionally go unaddressed by the Talker itself given the reasoning budget constraints necessitated by its priority on low-latency fluent dialogue. The Perception Agent addresses this limitation by reasoning over an extended video window, and maintaining a persistent memory of all clinical audio-visual cues detected over time. For example, if a patient exhibits a dry cough at the beginning of an interaction, the Perception Agent will log this observation and ensure it remains accessible to the system for subsequent clinical reasoning. The Perception Agent implements the same asynchronous relationship with the Talker Agent as described for the Planner Agent above.

### 2.2. Automated Evaluation

To guide development, we constructed an automated evaluation framework designed to assess system performance across a spectrum of clinical and conversational contexts relevant to real-time video telehealth settings (Section 2.2.1). The framework comprises two core paradigms: (1) targeted single-turn evaluations (Section 2.2.2), which isolate specific audio-visual capabilities; (2) simulated multi-turn interactions (Section 2.2.3), which assess end-to-end conversational capability as a proxy for eventual performance in the evaluation study.

### 2.2.1. Telehealth Evaluation Taxonomy

We first derived a taxonomy of clinical audio-visual cues and physical examination maneuvers relevant to telehealth settings (Section A.1). Synthesized from the medical literature and physical examination protocols [22–25], our taxonomy encompasses physical observations and guided examinations across major body systems and observation categories. We categorized the clinical audio-visual cues by their “telehealth feasibility”—whether they can be reasonably observed in a virtual setting—and by acquisition method, distinguishing between passive observations and those involving guided or elicited maneuvers.

For the purpose of this study, we further classified clinical signs into “actable” presentations (realistically simulated by patient actors, such as motor or behavioral changes) and “non-actable” presentations (specific physical or behavioral abnormalities that cannot be enacted).

### 2.2.2. Single-turn Evaluation

Single-turn agent evaluations served as ‘unit tests’ for specific audio-visual telehealth capabilities, including clinical perception, reasoning, and interaction. These scenarios were grounded in audio or video clips (sourced from publicly available materials and study-specific enactments) and designed to elicit specific internal reasoning or dialogue responses from the agent at precise points in a patient conversation. For instance, an evaluation scenario testing visual perception may depict a patient raising their right hand and asking, “what am I showing you?” The target response requires accurate identification of both anatomical location and laterality. Each evaluation case was paired with examplespecific clinical grading rubrics that describe the desired response and internal reasoning of the agent. During evaluation, an LLM-based auto-rater grades the agent’s response with a quality score from 0 to 1 applying the rubric. Further details on the design of single-turn agent evaluations are described in Section A.2.

### 2.2.3. Multi-turn Evaluation

While single-turn evaluation facilitates targeted benchmarking of perception, clinical encounters are inherently dynamic. For instance, while an agent should consistently elicit the anatomical location of a patient’s abdominal pain, the precise turn at which this request occurs may vary across conversations. To evaluate these conversational-level competencies, we leveraged multi-turn evaluations, evolving techniques from prior work with text-based simulated AI patients [10, 11], to an audio setting. In these simulations, visual physical examination cues were conveyed through injected verbal stage directions. For instance, if the agent instructs the patient to palpate their abdomen, the simulator might respond with the spoken audio confirmation, “Sure,” accompanied by the caption, “[patient presses on their lower right abdomen while simultaneously wincing].” This multi-turn evaluation was applied to the clinical scenarios used in Shah et al. [19], and an LLM-based auto-rater graded the clinical dialogue using case-specific rubrics across core clinical dimensions (history-taking, clinical reasoning, communication and counseling, treatment planning, triage, and red-flag identification).

### 2.3. OSCE Study

We conducted a randomized multi-arm evaluation study comparing AMIE with a group of US boardcertified primary care physicians (PCPs) for the task of conducting real-time video-based telehealth consultations with patient actors, including one study arm testing AMIE in its text chat configuration (Figure 3). We adapted the virtual Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) framework introduced in Tu et al. [11], designing a total of 120 scenario packs enriched with audio-visual cues and guided physical examination components. Complete study details, participant characteristics,

### 2.3.1. Study Design and Clinical Scenarios

A validation set of 20 clinical scenarios was used to conduct a study pilot with six arms comparing AMIE and PCPs in Video, Audio, and Text modalities each respectively, resulting in 120 completed consultations (6 across each of 20 scenarios). The purpose of this study pilot was to perform an initial validation of the agent and interface, and to inform the final study design through a small-scale ablation isolating effects of text, audio, and audio-video modalities. Details and results from the pilot are provided in Section A.5.

The full evaluation study was conducted across a distinct set of 100 clinical scenarios across three arms: AMIE (Video), AMIE (Text), and PCP (Video). All arms were conducted through a teleconferencing interface resembling Google Meet affording interactions through text chat and real-time audio-video modalities. (Figure A.4). In this study, AMIE did not feature a visual avatar. For controlled comparison and to avoid bias from visual presence or appearance, PCPs were asked to turn their cameras off throughout the consultations (Section A.6.1).

Scenario packs and simulated patients were prepared by an OSCE laboratory in North America and verified by US board-certified PCPs (Section A.6.2). Drawing from HHS resources for virtual care∗, scenarios were designed to span five clinical domains relevant to telehealth settings: (1) cardiopulmonary, (2) abdominal, (3) HEENT (head, eyes, ear, nose, throat), (4) neurology and psychiatry, and (5) musculoskeletal. Each of these categories included a subset of non-disease cases with resolved complaints to assess clinical reasoning and behavior in those negative settings. Inpatient, pediatric, and dermatological cases, as well as those with privacy-sensitive physical examinations were excluded. Each pack defined ground-truth diagnoses, plausible alternatives, investigations, management plans, and a 20-point rubric used to score clinical capability in case-specific manner (Section A.7).

Following each encounter, AMIE and PCPs produced answers to a structured post-questionnaire documenting differential diagnoses, observations, and management recommendations (Sections A.6.6 and A.9). For this post-encounter step, which operates under less stringent latency constraints than live dialogue, the AMIE system leveraged inference-time compute scaling via multi-draft synthesis [10] to improve recommendation quality.

### 2.3.2. Patient Actors and Primary Care Physicians

Clinical scenarios were enacted by a cohort of 15 professional patient actors (7 female, 8 male; ages 20–75) trained to deliver standardized portrayals of clinical affect, physical cues, and guided physical examination maneuvers matched to biological sex (Section A.6.3). Consultations in the PCP (Video) arm were performed by 10 US board-certified PCPs (mean 4.5 years post-residency clinical experience, Section A.6.5).

### 2.3.3. Evaluation Rubrics

Consultations were evaluated from multiple perspectives. Following each visit, patient actors evaluated conversational quality and communication convenience using established criteria from GMCPQ (General Medical Council Patient Questionnaire), PACES (Practical Assessment of Clinical Examination Skills), and PCCBP (Patient-Centered Communication Best Practice) adapted from Tu et al. ### 2.3.4. Qualitative Data

Patient actors and clinical evaluators were encouraged to leave free-text comments in their assessments to provide specific rationale for their ratings. To further characterize consultation experience from the patient actor perspective, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 7 patient actors, probing at differences in interaction modalities and conversational experience. Qualitative data was analyzed using an reflexive thematic analysis to inductively generate themes based on the transcripts and researcher notes. Details are provided in Section A.14.

### 2.3.5. Statistical Analysis

For the 20-point case-specific rubrics, performance was aggregated as the mean score earned out of the possible points achievable across each of the five core rubric categories, as well as overall. For ease of interpretation, Likert ratings from general assessment rubrics were standardized to a percentage scale for reporting (0% representing the lowest ratings for all 100 cases, and 100% representing the highest possible scores for all 100 cases). Differences across study arms were evaluated using a two-stage procedure: an omnibus Friedman test was first conducted to assess for differences across all three arms, followed by two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction for comparisons between pairs of arms. Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were conducted using scenario-level blocking. Cases with N/A ratings on either arm of a comparison were excluded. All 𝑝values reported in the manuscript refer to FDR adjusted p values from Wilcoxon signed rank tests. Error bars correspond to 95% confidence intervals produced via bootstrap procedure with 1000 resamples.

Video enabled direct demonstration of physical symptoms: Patient actors generally preferred video for physical complaints, noting that it allowed them to show rather than describe symptoms. As one actor explained, video enabled demonstrating specific movements versus “describing like I’m supinating my arm and it hurts. You can just show them and then they can interpret that” (P6). ### 3.4. Automated Evaluation Results

Automated evaluations characterized the contributions of individual agents to overall system performance and identified remaining capability gaps. Full results are provided in Sections A.3 and A.4.

Specialized agents meaningfully contributed to overall system performance: In single-turn evaluations, the full system achieved 59% compared with 42% for the Talker-only baseline. The Perception Agent provided the largest individual contribution, raising overall accuracy to 58%, with pronounced gains on visual inspection tasks such as abdominal distension, ascites, and wall contour (88% vs 33%) and eyelid lesions including chalazia, blepharitis, and ptosis (91% vs 56%). The Planner Agent complemented these perceptual capabilities through clinical reasoning, improving performance on tasks such as postural balance loss and gait instability (54% vs 32%) and joint range of motion and mobility limitations (65% vs 50%). In multi-turn simulated consultations across 20 clinical scenarios from [19], the Planner Agent yielded marked improvements in conversational quality and clinical thoroughness, with the full system scoring 87% on overall case-specific rubrics compared with 71% for the Talker-only ablation. These quality gains were achieved at substantially lower latency than the architecture described by Shah et al. [19], driven by the transition from sequential to asynchronous agent orchestration, reducing mean turn latency from 21.4s [95% CI: 20.3s, 23.0s] to 2.6s [95% CI: 2.3s, 2.8s].

Gaps remained in subtle and high-frequency perceptual competencies: Performance in automated evaluations varied considerably across clinical domains. Predominantly physical tasks achieved strong results (Pain behavior: 88%, Dermatologic: 75%, Musculoskeletal: 70%), while interactive domains such as Communication and behavior (44%) and Environment and setup (46%) proved more challenging. Key failure modes involved high-frequency or subtle audio-visual competencies, including nystagmus (3%), tremors at rest or with action (24%), and affective state, expressiveness, and mood congruence (29%).

## 4. Related Work

### 4.1. Foundation Models: From Language to Perception

The development of foundation models for generalist medical artificial intelligence [27] has progressed from static question-answering toward interactive clinical dialogue. Early clinical foundation models demonstrated expert-level medical question-answering on static benchmarks such as MedQA [28–33].

However, in medical training, written examinations do not reliably predict clinical competence [34, 35], as corroborated by the gap between AI performance on static benchmarks and in interactive clinical settings [36, 37]. In simulated text-based patient encounters, conversational AI systems have matched or exceeded primary care physicians (PCPs) in diagnostic reasoning, management recommendations, and perceived empathy across multi-turn text interactions [9–11]. In subspecialist domains, randomized and blinded evaluations showed that AI assistance reduced clinically significant errors among cardiologists in complex cardiovascular care [38] and produced management plans comparable to oncology fellows in breast cancer care [39]. Prospective clinical feasibility studies have begun to evaluate conversational agents in real-world ambulatory care, supporting their initial safety and decision-support utility [13–15], often under structured multi-agent clinician oversight [40, 41].

Yet text-based interfaces impose a communicative bottleneck that introduces reporting biases [16] and accessibility barriers [17, 18], while risking the omission of critical diagnostic cues. Multimodal clinical models have incorporated static medical imagery and offline data [12, 33, 42–44]. However, active clinical encounters require continuous, real-time audio-visual perception. While full-duplex speech-to-speech foundation models enable low-latency spoken dialogue [45–47], a disconnect between perception and action persists. Here, current voice systems can reliably identify vocal delivery cues such as distress or sarcasm when queried, but frequently disregard these paralinguistic signals during consequential decision-making [48]. Leveraging streaming audio-video infrastructure [49], Shah et al. [19] established the feasibility of an audio-visual medical AI across 20 proof-ofconcept scenarios demonstrating superiority of a Gemini-based system over a GPT-Realtime baseline, while highlighting important gaps to fill before reaching physician-level performance in this task. The present work builds on these foundations to provide the first demonstration of expert-level clinical performance in real-time video consultations.

### 4.2. Scaling Reasoning with Multi-Agent Architectures

Expert clinical practice requires balancing rapid conversational rapport with rigorous deliberative reasoning. In foundation models, scaling test-time compute via chain-of-thought prompting, selfconsistency, and search has been shown to substantially improve diagnostic accuracy [30, 31, 50–56]. However, while extensive search is well-suited to offline tasks, live clinical consultations impose strict conversational pacing (of only a few seconds of delay between turns), creating a fundamental tension between deep inference-time reasoning and real-time responsiveness.

Multi-agent architectures address this tension by decoupling fast conversational interaction from slower, deliberative reasoning [10, 40, 56, 57]. Polaris [40] employed specialized clinical agents to monitor conversational safety, while Christakopoulou et al. [57] pioneered a dual-agent “System 1” (Talker) and “System 2” (Reasoner) architecture. Similar tandem designs have emerged in real-time speech systems to anchor low-latency spoken dialogue with deliberative knowledge retrieval [58, 59]. Building on the Talker-Reasoner paradigm applied to text-based longitudinal disease management [10], AMIE (Video) extends this architecture to real-time audio-visual streaming: a 3-agent harness (Talker, Planner, and Perception) that executes deep clinical reasoning and continuous perceptual analysis asynchronously, without interrupting fluid dialogue.

### 4.3. Telehealth Examination and Evaluation

In clinical practice, visual and auditory observations are fundamental aspects of history-taking and physical assessment that cannot be replaced through text [5]. The growth of telemedicine has established the virtual physical examination as a viable clinical discipline, demonstrating that key maneuvers across musculoskeletal, neurological, dermatological, and respiratory systems can be guided effectively over video [7, 8, 22–24]. Moreover, comparative telehealth studies show that video consultations significantly improve diagnostic demonstration and patient satisfaction over audio-only visits [6].

Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) [60] remains the gold standard examination format to evaluate clinical competence during medical training, with candidates conducting consultations with professional patient actors, so-called ‘standardized patients’ to complete a series of pre-defined clinical tasks [61]. Medical educators have adapted OSCEs to virtual encounters [26], suggesting rubrics for telehealth communication and diagnostic process. While prior studies have used OSCE frameworks to evaluate text-based and static multimodal AI [10–12, 41], comprehensive assessment benefits from pairing holistic communication scales with granular, case-specific clinical checklists [62], an approach aligned with contemporary medical dialogue benchmarking [19, 63, 64] and adopted in our video-based OSCE study.

## 5. Discussion

Audio-visual capabilities are essential for AI systems to overcome the fundamental diagnostic and communicative bottlenecks of text-only interfaces. Text-based interactions place a heavy burden on patients to translate complex somatic sensations and physical abnormalities into written words, a dependency that often leads to missed cues or ambiguity. In contrast, multimodal audio-video communication unlocks a rich, real-time stream of objective clinical data. It captures nuanced auditory signals, including respiratory effort, vocal strain, and emotional affect, while enabling direct observation of visual signs such as diaphoresis, scleral icterus, and acute distress. Furthermore, live audio-visual interaction can enable improved clinical rapport and the dynamic guidance of patients through interactive physical examination maneuvers (e.g., abdominal self-palpation, active range of motion, capillary refill) with substantially higher diagnostic fidelity.

The AMIE (Video) system represents a step change from text-bound diagnostic agents to a synchronous, audio-visual interaction. It is the first such system to demonstrate PCP-level performance in a randomized OSCE study setting, as rated by independent clinical evaluators. For many evaluation domains, including case-specific history taking, clinical reasoning, treatment planning, and patient communication, clinical evaluators rated AMIE’s performance as significantly better than the baseline PCPs. AMIE (Video) was also preferred for its more proactive approach to physical examination and observation. Patient actors generally rated AMIE’s conversational capabilities favorably compared with those of PCPs, rating AMIE (Video) higher for assessing and explaining their condition. These higher ratings were achieved within a similar encounter duration (8.9 vs. 9.3 minutes), a notable finding given that longer visit times are strongly linked to increased patient satisfaction and more effective management of chronic and psychosocial conditions [65, 66].

These comparative findings are meaningful because the human baseline in this study was designed to closely reflect an actual clinical practice setting. Video-based telemedicine is widely utilized and continues to grow as a standard interaction modality. Prior studies of text-based conversational medical AI [10–12, 15, 41] may underestimate physician performance because physicians are more accustomed to telephone or video-based consultation [67, 68]. This work was designed to be more representative of video-based telemedicine, with PCPs able to see and hear the patient using a familiar

video conferencing interface. The PCP baseline in this study therefore serves as a stronger proxy for real-world clinical practice, though key differences remain. Most notably, the study used patient actors instead of actual patients, and physicians were required to keep their cameras off.

Clinical evaluators also rated AMIE (Video) higher than PCPs for its proactivity in guiding physical examinations. In this study, human physicians often leaned on oral history-taking rather than instructing patients to perform active examination maneuvers. This difference may reflect clinicians defaulting to in-person consultation habits, where physical exams are typically performed in the clinic rather than coached remotely. AMIE, by contrast, systematically prompted patients through step-by-step physical examination maneuvers. This behavior highlights a potential opportunity for AI systems, which are less inhibited by traditional time constraints, to elicit more thorough clinical information during virtual care. Indeed, it has been shown that many physical assessment maneuvers can be successfully adapted to synchronous video encounters [7, 8, 24]. However, further research is needed to understand the clinical necessity and diagnostic yield of such maneuvers relative to the additional time, effort, and cognitive load required from the patient.

The AMIE (Text) arm served as a useful ablation to characterize the impact of audio-visual interaction. Patient actors significantly preferred the audio-visual communication for its ease of use, communicative effectiveness, and ability to make the user of the system feel understood. Clinical evaluators rated AMIE (Video) as superior to AMIE (Text) in several domains key to the telehealth setting, such as fostering a relationship, audio-visual perception, and guided examination, as well as overall across all five case-specific clinical rubrics in aggregate. However, for rubrics related to clinical reasoning such as diagnostic and management appropriateness, AMIE (Video) was comparable to AMIE (Text). In part, this may reflect a trend towards approaching saturation on these simulated OSCE scenarios, where text-based clinical reasoning performance is already high. This finding also aligns with clinical literature suggesting that the medical history alone establishes the correct diagnosis in the vast majority of outpatient encounters, while physical examination alters the primary diagnosis in only a small fraction of cases [69, 70]. Similar results have been observed in other recent telehealth studies, showing comparable clinical effectiveness between telephone and video consultations [71], though other studies have identified reductions in medication errors and improved diagnostic accuracy [72] with the addition of video. Because a missed visual cue can often be compensated by verbal questioning, the distinct advantages of audio-visual reasoning may only emerge in specific situations, such as when a patient’s spoken statements conflict with visual evidence (e.g., verbally naming one medication while holding up a different pill bottle). These simulated scenarios were designed to reflect a breadth of telehealth settings including opportunities for physical observation and examination. However, they were not designed to render purely text-based consultations impossible, which helps to contextualize this finding.

The granular, case-specific rubrics (Section A.6.9) were designed to more precisely detect nuanced variations in clinical performance and communication that the broader general rubrics may overlook. As clinical agents improve and metrics like diagnostic accuracy become more saturated, these targeted scoring criteria, which can be tailored to the precise challenges of each scenario, may help uncover more subtle differences in clinical competency. This approach mirrors recent shifts in medical LLM evaluation, such as HealthBench [63, 64], which evaluates open-ended responses to clinical dialogues against physician-authored conversation-specific rubrics. In OSCE examinations used in medical education, station-specific checklists are often utilized [60]; combining general clinical rubrics with case-specific criteria ensures a balanced and standardized assessment of the overall conversational appropriateness and clinical reasoning [62].

The real-time delivery of high-quality dialogue from AMIE was enabled by its decoupled, asynchronous multi-agent architecture. This design addresses a fundamental tension in real-time medical

dialogue: the need for near-instantaneous conversational turn-taking (low latency) versus the computational expense of thorough diagnostic reasoning and continuous visual processing. Automated evaluation ablations confirm that this three-agent harness substantially outperforms the single-agent baseline and prior harnesses from Shah et al. [19], while operating at a natural conversational latency (around 3 seconds per turn). These ablations also show how individual components of AMIE (Video) meaningfully contribute to overall system performance.

A rigorous offline evaluation framework is essential for systematically benchmarking agent performance and tracking progress throughout development. Our evaluation framework comprises two components: the clinical audio-visual taxonomy (Section A.1) and a multi-tiered benchmark suite. Grounded in telehealth feasibility, the taxonomy defines a principled spectrum of audio-visual signs that can be elicited and interpreted in virtual care. While exhaustively covering every clinical action and condition in the taxonomy was beyond the scope of this work, our approach establishes an extensible blueprint for evaluating multimodal clinical AI. Specifically, we pair complementary single-turn benchmarks, which isolate and evaluate discrete instances of clinical perception and diagnostic reasoning, with multi-turn simulated consultations that assess holistic, conversation-level competencies. Together, these tiers provide a computationally and logistically scalable proxy for the evaluation of real-time clinical audio-video consultations. Although the present multi-turn audio simulation communicates visual cues descriptively, future evaluation environments can directly incorporate dynamically generated synthetic patient videos [73].

While the agents in AMIE (Video) are orchestrated through prompting, multi-turn reinforcement learning with simulated patients has been shown to yield robust improvements in diagnostic accuracy and clinical safety [74]. The simulated encounters and structured evaluation criteria developed in this work could serve as a training environment for such end-to-end optimization.

### 5.1. Limitations

The system described in this work is not ready for real-world clinical deployment and several core limitations must be acknowledged. An important architectural constraint of AMIE (Video) is its reliance on discrete turn-taking rather than continuous, multi-stream interactivity. Although the decoupled multi-agent design balances conversational latency and reasoning by running background agents asynchronously, the ultimate interaction loop still hinges on more rigid turn boundaries. Consequently, the patient and agent cannot speak simultaneously or engage in rapid, overlapping back-and-forth dialogue as human clinicians and patients naturally do during consultations. Furthermore, this audio-based separation also prevents visually triggered interjections, such as speaking up to guide a patient actor who is improperly executing a physical examination maneuver. Recent paradigms, such as interaction models [75], multi-stream LLMs [59], and tandem speech architectures like KAME [58], address these sequential bottlenecks by enabling full-duplex communication (“speaking while listening”).

Despite the strong end-to-end performance AMIE (Video) demonstrated in our OSCE evaluation study, automated evaluations uncover important capability gaps that warrant careful examination. Subtle affective nuances and high-frequency movements like tremor remain difficult for the agent to reliably perceive. These granular perceptual capabilities are crucial to clinical reasoning for some medical presentations and therefore should be further developed in future work to increase robustness and coverage of audio-visual perceptive capabilities. Additionally, even when an agent successfully perceives subtle non-verbal cues, it may still fail to translate this perception into appropriate clinical action. During automated evaluations, we observed instances where the agent’s perception was accurate, yet did not trigger the appropriate proactive response (such as noticing poor audio quality but failing to request a correction). This mirrors other recent findings which demonstrate that voice

agents can recognize properties like distress or sarcasm but fall short of fully incorporating them in their decision-making [48].

Constructing and executing automated evaluations for complex interactive domains like audiovisual clinical consultations is a process with inherent challenges. Patient-acted videos exhibit varying degrees of clinical realism, while internet-sourced videos can lack the focused and natural presentation typical of live telehealth encounters. Furthermore, evaluating perception, reasoning, and interactivity in a targeted single-turn manner involved designing occasionally contrived examples (e.g., a patient directly asking, “It hurts right here... what part is this?”) to strictly isolate the capability being tested. Additionally, while we included a limited number of ‘adversarial’ examples, future iterations of the framework may enrich this adversarial subset with additional scenarios, such as patient actors performing examination maneuvers incorrectly or contradicting physical observations. During automated evaluation, the patient simulator’s behavior can vary slightly across simulation runs, and auto-graders exhibit a certain degree of intra-rater variability. Therefore, performance comparisons stemming from this automated process should be interpreted with appropriate caution. While automated evaluation results are valuable for relative comparisons of multiple candidate systems, their calibration with clinical evaluator ratings may not be precise. Consequently, these automated evaluations were primarily used to assess directional improvements of the system as sub-components were added or improved. However, they are not a suitable replacement for rigorous randomized studies involving human physician comparisons, professional patient actors and evaluation ratings from independent clinical evaluators.

The clinical scope of the scenarios selected for the OSCE study were limited. Because evaluations relied entirely on live enactments by professional patient actors, the 100 study scenarios were restricted to “actable” clinical presentations. Consequently, important clinical scenarios featuring core audio-visual diagnostic components such as dermatological conditions that cannot be authentically simulated by actors were omitted from the study. Furthermore, while patient actors provide a useful standardized baseline for comparative evaluation, real-world clinical encounters introduce unscripted behavioral, environmental, and emotional complexities.

A related constraint involved demographic alignment between patient actors and the simulated clinical conditions. While experimental protocols successfully matched actor biological sex to the clinical case descriptions and maintained a broad distribution across racial backgrounds and age groups, this challenge was particularly pronounced in simulating complex chronic and acute illnesses that disproportionately affect geriatric populations (e.g., severe cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). This skew reflects logistical constraints in recruiting older standardized patients as well as the digital literacy required for synchronous teleconferencing platforms which remains a documented barrier to telemedicine access among older populations [76–78]. Evaluating conversational AI with older patient cohorts who present with multi-morbidity and sensory or cognitive impairments is an essential next step for clinical generalizability.

While our experimental protocol implemented several measures to standardize conditions between study arms, complete blinding remained challenging. Standardization measures included utilizing an identical teleconferencing interface (capable of video interaction and text chat modalities) across all arms, asking PCPs to turn off their own camera during consultations to match the avatar-less AI system, and randomizing scenario presentation order and evaluation sequence across arms. Limitations to blinding include the synthetic vocal style of the Talker agent which remains audibly distinct from human physician speech, and the fact that the text-only arm represented an inherently different interaction format. Such unblinding is a critical consideration, as awareness of an agent’s AI identity can directly affect user behavior; it was observed in Reis et al. [79] that patients who believe they are interacting with an AI chatbot rather than a physician demonstrate lower-quality symptom reports.
